title: Hadges v. Yonkers Racing Corp.
lead: A harness driver failed to reopen an earlier judgment for fraud, but defects in the sanctions proceedings required separate relief for him and his lawyer.

actors.name: George Hadges
actors.role: Harness driver, trainer, and owner excluded from Yonkers Raceway

proceedings: The 1990 § 1983 judgment for YRC was affirmed.
District court denied an independent fraud-on-the-court action and imposed a $2,000 client sanction and attorney censure.
Second Circuit affirmed denial of relief and reversed both sanctions.
limits: This account applies the 1993 Rule 11 amendment and historical Rule 60 savings clause. The recusal refusal was not appealed. The appellate court did not reopen exclusion merits or reach disputed preclusion and abstention alternatives.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: A licensed driver loses access to Yonkers
sections.cue: The first federal judgment turns on state action
paragraphs: George Hadges worked as a harness driver, trainer, and owner. His racing license, first issued in 1972, was revoked in 1974 for incomplete arrest disclosure and restored in 1976. In 1989 it was suspended for six months after a determination that he improperly passed wagering information at a 1986 race. When his license returned in September 1989, Yonkers Racing Corporation independently refused him access to its track.

Hadges sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for denial of due process. In 1990 the district court granted the company summary judgment because its action was not state action; the judgment was affirmed. Track manager Galterio stated that other regional tracks remained available. The district court suggested concerted exclusion by other tracks might establish state action.

A 1992 New York suit alleging blackballing and other claims failed. A separate federal suit against the state-run Meadowlands began in 1993 and settled. Meadowlands manager Garland explained that a 1992 resolution allowed it to exclude drivers barred elsewhere. Hadges then sought to reopen the 1990 judgment through an independent fraud-on-the-court action, treating Garland’s affidavit as proof Galterio’s earlier account was fraudulent.

sections.title: Disputed statements generate sanctions
paragraphs: Hadges said he had not worked for more than four years. Yonkers produced records of five Monticello races in 1991 and seven in 1993. Hadges acknowledged those appearances while explaining their minimal earnings. He also submitted an undated scratch sheet supporting an asserted 1989 exclusion by state racing judges. Yonkers established that it concerned 1987. Hadges corrected the date and provided affidavits about a different asserted 1989 incident; attorney William Kunstler said he had not known the first date was wrong.

The district court denied reopening, fined Hadges $2,000 for misrepresentations, and censured Kunstler for inadequate investigation and failing to disclose pending state litigation. Yonkers had requested sanctions within its dismissal papers, without a separate motion served twenty-one days before presentation. The amended Rule 11 had taken effect five days before the complaint and fifteen days before the request.

sections.title: Fraud on the court is not established
sections.cue: The later exclusion does not prove an earlier falsehood
paragraphs: Judge Feinberg, writing for the Second Circuit panel with Judges Kearse and Altimari, first affirmed denial of relief. More than a year had passed, preventing a timely Rule 60(b)(3) motion, but the historical savings clause allowed an independent action for fraud upon the court. That narrow category required serious damage to adjudicative integrity, not merely fraud against an opponent.

Meadowlands adopted its resolution and excluded Hadges in 1992, after the 1990 litigation. Galterio denied knowing otherwise, and Hadges offered no persuasive contrary evidence. A state track’s later reliance on a private track’s exclusion did not show conspiracy or concerted blackballing by all New York tracks. Although the action was not frivolous, it did not approach the necessary impairment of adjudication. The court therefore found no abuse of discretion without reaching disputed res judicata or abstention grounds.

sections.title: The failed lawsuit does not validate defective sanctions
paragraphs: The 1993 amendment required reasonable inquiry and evidentiary support, replacing the older certification formulation. Its separate-motion and safe-harbor safeguards allowed correction or withdrawal before sanctions were sought from the court. The defects in those safeguards mattered here. Hadges acknowledged Monticello appearances in an affidavit sworn twelve days after the sanctions request. He and Kunstler corrected the scratch-sheet date soon after the judge indicated sanctions were under consideration; sanctions did not rest on whether the replacement 1989 account was true. A proper correction opportunity could have avoided punishment. The opinion noted an apparently erroneous filing stamp without treating it as an accurate filing date.

The district court also relied on an allegedly unwarranted disqualification motion. Amended Rule 11 barred the specified monetary legal-contention sanction against a represented party. Court-initiated sanctions could not cure the problem: the judge said he acted on Yonkers’ request and issued no required specific show-cause order. The panel doubted the conduct approached the contempt-like situation contemplated for that route. The recusal refusal itself was not appealed.

Kunstler lacked the same safe harbor. His reliance also had an objective evidentiary basis: sworn client information, the undated sheet, another lawyer’s affidavit, and his experience in the Meadowlands litigation. Much of the dating evidence belonged to Yonkers. The court did not excuse unquestioning repetition of every client statement. It also noted that Yonkers misleadingly suggested nearly $2,000 in earnings, while the uncontroverted driver earnings were under $100.

State-case nondisclosure was absent from the judge’s sanctions notice, and Yonkers’ request was defective. The blackballing issue had not been adjudicated on its merits, and Yonkers could disclose its own litigation. Disclosure would have been wiser but did not justify censure here. Personal remarks about Kunstler, activist lawyers, and unrelated conduct by his partner further supported reversal.

With no separate writing, the Second Circuit affirmed the denial of reopening and reversed both Hadges’s $2,000 sanction and Kunstler’s censure. Hadges won relief from sanctions, not a new adjudication of his exclusion.
